etymology: Old English hebban, to lift or raise. Webster 1828: to lift; to raise; to move upward. In the Authorized Version the word is almost entirely technical: the heave offering is the portion of a sacrifice lifted up before the LORD and then assigned to the priest, and it is paired throughout with the wave offering.
biblical_def: A heave offering is not a mood and not a sigh. It is a legal portion of a sacrifice, lifted up in the presence of the LORD and thereby transferred from the worshipper to the priest who serves at the altar. Of the peace offerings, the right shoulder shall ye give unto the priest for an heave offering (Leviticus 7:32), and of the whole oblation one cake is offered for an heave offering unto the LORD, and it shall be the priest’s that sprinkleth the blood (Leviticus 7:14). The lifting is the point. What is heaved is publicly removed from common use and set where God directs it. So the firstfruits of the dough are heaved (Numbers 15:20), and the Levites in their turn heave a tenth of the tithe they receive: Thus ye also shall offer an heave offering unto the LORD of all your tithes (Numbers 18:28). Even the Nazarite’s completion involves the wave breast and heave shoulder (Numbers 6:20). The dictionary keeps the word technical because Scripture keeps it technical. A heave offering is the visible answer to the question of who owns the increase, and the answer is always the same: the LORD owns it, and He assigns a portion of it to the men who stand before Him on the people’s behalf.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HEAVE as to lift; to raise; to move upward; also, to raise or force from the breast, as a sigh. The biblical technical sense — an offering lifted up and thereby consecrated — stands directly on the primary meaning of lifting.
webster_full: HEAVE, v.t. — To lift; to raise; to move upward. To cause to swell or rise. To raise or force from the breast; as, to heave a sigh.
HEAVE, n. — A rising or swell; an effort upward; a lift.
Webster’s primary sense is the biblical one. The offering is named for the motion made over it: it is lifted, in sight of the congregation, out of the offerer’s hand and into the LORD’s claim.
scriptures: Leviticus 7:14
And of it he shall offer one out of the whole oblation for an heave offering unto the LORD, and it shall be the priest's that sprinkleth the blood of the peace offerings.
Leviticus 7:32
And the right shoulder shall ye give unto the priest for an heave offering of the sacrifices of your peace offerings.
Numbers 15:20
Ye shall offer up a cake of the first of your dough for an heave offering: as ye do the heave offering of the threshingfloor, so shall ye heave it.
Numbers 18:28
Thus ye also shall offer an heave offering unto the LORD of all your tithes, which ye receive of the children of Israel; and ye shall give thereof the LORD'S heave offering to Aaron the priest.
Numbers 6:20
And the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD: this is holy for the priest, with the wave breast and heave shoulder: and after that the Nazarite may drink wine.
corruption_summary: The heave offering is corrupted whenever giving is emptied of its object — when the lifting up before the LORD is replaced by a transaction between a donor and an institution, and when the portion assigned to those who minister is treated as either a salary or an embarrassment.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the emptying of the direction. A heave offering is lifted unto the LORD; only then is it given to the priest. Strip out the first movement and the second becomes mere subscription, a fee paid to a religious organization for services rendered. Leviticus 7:14 will not permit it: the cake is offered unto the LORD, and it belongs to the priest that sprinkleth the blood — the man standing in the place of atonement, not the man running an office. The New Testament keeps the logic when Paul argues from the altar that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14). The support of ministers is a consequence of God’s claim on the increase, not a market price.

The second corruption is the tenth of the tenth. Numbers 18:28 requires the Levites themselves to heave an offering out of what they receive. Those who live from the offerings of God’s people are not thereby exempt from offering; they are the first to be measured. Where ministry becomes a class that receives and never gives, or where a church treats its receipts as its own capital, the pattern of Numbers 18 has been abandoned. The heave offering makes stewardship visible at every link in the chain, and it stops at no one.
roots_summary: The Hebrew noun behind heave offering is terumah, from a verb meaning to lift up or raise high. It is the standing Old Testament word for a contribution set apart by being lifted, and it is used both of sanctuary materials and of sacrificial portions.
roots_lines: Hebrew terumah (H8641) — a heave offering; a contribution lifted out and set apart (Leviticus 7:14; Numbers 15:20; Numbers 18:28).
Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, to rise, to lift up; the root motion from which terumah is named.
The paired word is tenuphah, the wave offering, moved horizontally rather than lifted — the two motions appear together in Numbers 6:20 and Exodus 29:27.
The same terumah names the materials lifted out for building the tabernacle (Exodus 25:2-3), which is why the word covers both worship and construction.
English heave renders the motion, not the emotion; the KJV never uses it of feeling in the sacrificial contexts.
usage: An heave offering unto the LORD (Leviticus 7:14) — lifted before God first, assigned to the priest second; the order is never reversed.
As ye do the heave offering of the threshingfloor, so shall ye heave it (Numbers 15:20) — the firstfruits of the dough follow the pattern of the grain.
The wave breast and heave shoulder (Numbers 6:20) — the two motions together, the standing portion of the priesthood.

etymology: From twine, to twist together, Old English twin, double thread. Webster 1828: twisted; convolved. In the Authorized Version the word appears almost exclusively in the phrase fine twined linen, the thread of the tabernacle: linen spun and doubled and twisted before it was ever woven.
biblical_def: Fine twined linen is the standing material of the sanctuary, and the adjective is doing real work. The thread is not simply fine; it has been twisted, doubled upon itself, so that what hangs in the court is strong as well as white. The curtains of the court on the south side were hangings for the court of fine twined linen of an hundred cubits long (Exodus 27:9), and the whole enclosure the same: All the hangings of the court round about were of fine twined linen (Exodus 38:16). The priests’ garments are cut from it — linen breeches of fine twined linen (Exodus 39:28) — and so are the inner curtains with their cherubim. Two things follow. First, the boundary between the camp and the holy place is made of the whitest and strongest thing Israel could produce, which is a sermon in cloth: what separates a sinner from God is purity, and purity is not flimsy. Second, God specified the thread. He did not merely command a fence; He named the fibre, the doubling, and the colours worked into it. The regulative principle of worship has a textile in the Old Testament: God says how, and not only that.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives TWINE as to twist; to wind or unite closely; and TWINED as twisted or convolved. The biblical phrase is exact: a thread twisted double before weaving, which is what makes fine linen both fine and strong.
webster_full: TWINE, v.t. — To twist; to wind, as one thread around another. To unite closely; to embrace.
TWINED, pp. — Twisted; convolved; wound about.

The doubling is the whole force of the word. A single fine thread would be delicate; a fine thread twined is fine and durable together, which is precisely what a hanging exposed to weather and a garment worn in service both require.
scriptures: Exodus 27:9
And thou shalt make the court of the tabernacle: for the south side southward there shall be hangings for the court of fine twined linen of an hundred cubits long for one side:
Exodus 27:18
The length of the court shall be an hundred cubits, and the breadth fifty every where, and the height five cubits of fine twined linen, and their sockets of brass.
Exodus 38:16
All the hangings of the court round about were of fine twined linen.
Exodus 39:28
And a mitre of fine linen, and goodly bonnets of fine linen, and linen breeches of fine twined linen,
Exodus 38:9
And he made the court: on the south side southward the hangings of the court were of fine twined linen, an hundred cubits:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure on fine twined linen is not redefinition but impatience — the modern habit of treating God’s specifications for worship as decorative detail rather than as command.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody is contesting the meaning of twined thread. What is contested, constantly, is whether God’s stated particulars in worship are binding or merely illustrative. Chapters of Exodus specify the fibre, the twist, the colours, the cubits, and the sockets, and they specify them twice — once as command and once as compliance. That doubling in the text is not padding. It is the record that Israel did it as it was said.

The principle to recover is the regulative principle of worship: what God commands in His worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not ours to add. The tabernacle is the clearest case in Scripture of a God who cares about the how. When a congregation reasons that the details of worship are matters of taste because the tabernacle details seem small, it has drawn exactly the wrong conclusion from Exodus. The smallness of the detail is the proof of the seriousness of the claim.
roots_summary: The Hebrew is a passive participle meaning twisted, from a root for twisting or spinning, standing with the word for fine white linen. The phrase is fixed: fine linen, twisted.
roots_lines: Hebrew shazar (H7806) — to twist, to twine; the passive participle yields twined in the phrase fine twined linen.
Hebrew shesh (H8336) — fine white linen, byssus; the fibre itself (Exodus 27:9; Exodus 38:16).
The fixed phrase shesh moshzar occurs throughout Exodus 26-39 for the curtains, the hangings, the ephod, and the priestly breeches.
Later Hebrew uses buts for fine linen in Chronicles and Esther; the Exodus material keeps shesh.
Greek byssos renders the fibre in the Septuagint and stands behind the fine linen, clean and white of Revelation 19:8.
usage: Hangings for the court of fine twined linen (Exodus 27:9) — the boundary of the holy place is white and doubled.
All the hangings of the court round about were of fine twined linen (Exodus 38:16) — the command in chapter 27 and the compliance in chapter 38 are recorded word for word.
Linen breeches of fine twined linen (Exodus 39:28) — the same thread that walls the court clothes the men who serve inside it.

etymology: From Latin oraculum, a divine utterance or the place where it is given, from orare, to speak or pray. Webster 1828: the answer of a god; the place where such answers were given. In the Authorized Version the word is chiefly architectural: the oracle is the innermost room of Solomon’s temple, the most holy place, where the ark stood.
biblical_def: In the English Bible oracle is not a fortune and not a medium. It is a room. Solomon built them for it within, even for the oracle, even for the most holy place (1 Kings 6:16), and its purpose is stated without ornament: And the oracle he prepared in the house within, to set there the ark of the covenant of the LORD (1 Kings 6:19). Within it stood two cherubims of olive tree, each ten cubits high (1 Kings 6:23). The name fits because that is where God had said He would speak — from above the mercy seat, from between the cherubim — so the room is called by the speech that issues from it. The worshipper outside prays toward it: when I lift up my hands toward thy holy oracle (Psalm 28:2). The one other use exposes the counterfeit. Ahithophel’s counsel was received as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God (2 Samuel 16:23) — a man’s advice given the weight of God’s speech, which is the standing temptation of every age. Scripture’s oracle has an address, a covenant, and a blood-sprinkled seat. It does not float.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ORACLE as the answer of a god or of an inspired person; the place where such answers were given; and, in Scripture, the sanctuary or most holy place of the temple. Webster preserves both the utterance and the room.
webster_full: ORACLE, n. [L. oraculum, from oro, to utter.] — Among pagans, the answer of a god, or of some person reputed to be a god, to an inquiry; also, the place where such answers were given.
In Scripture, the sanctuary or most holy place of the temple, in which was deposited the ark of the covenant, and where God gave His answers to the high priest.
Also, the communications, revelations or messages delivered by God to prophets, and hence the Scriptures themselves — as the oracles of God (Romans 3:2).
Webster’s three senses are the biblical progression: God speaks; the place He speaks from is named for the speaking; and the record of what He spoke is called the oracles of God.
scriptures: 1 Kings 6:16
And he built twenty cubits on the sides of the house, both the floor and the walls with boards of cedar: he even built them for it within, even for the oracle, even for the most holy place.
1 Kings 6:19
And the oracle he prepared in the house within, to set there the ark of the covenant of the LORD.
1 Kings 6:23
And within the oracle he made two cherubims of olive tree, each ten cubits high.
Psalm 28:2
Hear the voice of my supplications, when I cry unto thee, when I lift up my hands toward thy holy oracle.
2 Samuel 16:23
And the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God: so was all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom.
corruption_summary: Oracle is corrupted when it is detached from the covenant room and floated free — into pagan divination on one side, and on the other into the modern claim that a man’s impressions carry the authority of God’s speech.
corruption_paragraphs: The pagan corruption is the older one and Scripture names it plainly. Delphi, the Urim consulted by an apostate, the necromancer at Endor, and the liver-reading of Ezekiel 21:21 are all attempts to extract divine speech without covenant, without blood, and without obedience. The biblical oracle is the opposite in every particular: God fixes the place, prescribes the mercy seat, requires the blood, and appoints the man who may enter. Divination seeks information; the oracle of God gives a word to a people He has bound Himself to.

The live corruption is 2 Samuel 16:23 repeated. Ahithophel’s counsel was treated as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God, and the narrative that follows is the destruction that follows the confusion. Where the modern prophetic movement teaches believers to receive a leader’s impressions, dreams, or “words” with the weight owed only to Scripture, the sin is not enthusiasm but substitution. The canon is closed; the oracles of God are written; and every impression is to be measured by them rather than laid alongside them. Hebrews 1:1-2 settles the era: God who spoke by the prophets hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.
roots_summary: The Hebrew word rendered oracle in Kings is debir, the innermost room, related to the word for speaking. The Greek New Testament word for the Scriptures as God’s utterances is logia, the oracles of God.
roots_lines: Hebrew debir (H1687) — the innermost sanctuary, the most holy place (1 Kings 6:16, 19, 23); traditionally connected with dabar, to speak.
Hebrew dabar (H1696) — to speak; the room is named for the speech that comes out of it.
Greek logion (G3051) — an utterance of God; plural, the oracles of God committed to the Jews (Romans 3:2) and the standard for a preacher’s speech (1 Peter 4:11).
The Septuagint at 1 Kings uses dabir as a loanword, keeping the Hebrew architectural term rather than importing the pagan Greek manteion.
English oracle comes through Latin oraculum and carries the pagan sense natively; the KJV redeems it by fixing it to a room in Solomon’s temple.
usage: Even for the oracle, even for the most holy place (1 Kings 6:16) — the KJV supplies its own gloss; the oracle is a room, not a voice in the air.
I lift up my hands toward thy holy oracle (Psalm 28:2) — prayer has a direction because revelation had an address.
As if a man had enquired at the oracle of God (2 Samuel 16:23) — the standing warning against giving a counsellor the authority of Scripture.

etymology: Middle English kidenei, of uncertain formation. Webster 1828: the two glandular bodies in the lower part of the abdomen which secrete the urine. In the Authorized Version the word belongs almost entirely to the sacrificial law — the two kidneys with their fat are burned upon the altar — and once, figuratively, to the richest part of the wheat.
biblical_def: The kidneys are what God claims from the inside of the animal. The formula runs unchanged through Leviticus: And the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away (Leviticus 3:4), and again at Leviticus 4:9, and again at Leviticus 7:4. When the priests were consecrated the same parts were taken: the caul above the liver, and the two kidneys, and their fat, and Moses burned it upon the altar (Leviticus 8:16). What is burned is the deepest and richest interior of the sacrifice, the part no worshipper sees and no one eats. That is the doctrine. God is not satisfied with the visible surrender; He requires what is hidden. Scripture elsewhere uses the kidneys (rendered reins in the KJV) for the inmost self that God alone examines. The figure runs the other way too: Israel is fed with the fat of kidneys of wheat (Deuteronomy 32:14), the choicest of the grain. And in judgment the sword of the LORD is made fat with fatness… with the fat of the kidneys of rams (Isaiah 34:6), the sacrificial vocabulary turned against a nation that would not sacrifice.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines KIDNEY as one of the two glandular bodies which secrete the urine, and notes the figurative English use for sort or temperament. The biblical use is sacrificial and, through the KJV’s reins, moral: the hidden inward parts.
webster_full: KIDNEY, n. — The kidneys are two glandular bodies, situated in the lower part of the abdomen, one on each side, whose office is to secrete the urine.
Also used figuratively in English for sort, kind, or temperament — a man of that kidney.

The Authorized Version renders the same Hebrew word reins when the sense is moral rather than anatomical, as in the LORD trieth the hearts and reins — which keeps Webster’s two senses joined: the innermost organ, and the innermost man.
scriptures: Leviticus 3:4
And the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away.
Leviticus 4:9
And the two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away,
Leviticus 8:16
And he took all the fat that was upon the inwards, and the caul above the liver, and the two kidneys, and their fat, and Moses burned it upon the altar.
Deuteronomy 32:14
Butter of kine, and milk of sheep, with fat of lambs, and rams of the breed of Bashan, and goats, with the fat of kidneys of wheat; and thou didst drink the pure blood of the grape.
Isaiah 34:6

The sword of the LORD is filled with blood, it is made fat with fatness, and with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams: for the LORD hath a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Idumea.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure here is squeamishness — the modern instinct to skip Leviticus as primitive butchery — and the loss of the doctrine that God claims the hidden interior and not the presentable exterior.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No movement is redefining the kidneys. What is happening is quieter: whole congregations have never heard Leviticus read, and preachers who do read it hurry past the anatomy as though it were an embarrassment inherited from a cruder age. The repetition is deliberate. Four times in four chapters the same interior parts are named, and the effect on a reader who does not skip is cumulative — God specified what He would have burned, down to the fat beside the flanks.

The principle to recover is that God requires the inward parts. The same Hebrew word the sacrificial law uses for the kidneys the psalmists use for the seat of the affections, which the KJV renders reins: Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart (Psalm 26:2). A religion of surfaces has always been available, and Leviticus 3 forecloses it. If the altar took the kidneys and the caul, then the God of the altar is not content with the parts of a man that show.
roots_summary: The Hebrew noun is kilyah, the kidneys; the KJV renders it kidneys in sacrificial contexts and reins where the sense is the inmost self. It is the standard Old Testament figure for what only God can examine.
roots_lines: Hebrew kilyah (H3629) — kidneys; used of the sacrificial portions (Leviticus 3:4; 4:9; 8:16) and figuratively of the innermost man.
The KJV translates the same word reins at Psalm 7:9, Psalm 26:2, and Jeremiah 11:20 — the LORD trieth the hearts and reins.
Hebrew cheleb (H2459) — the fat; forbidden as food (Leviticus 3:17) because it is the LORD’s portion on the altar.
The figurative fat of kidneys of wheat (Deuteronomy 32:14) transfers the sacrificial vocabulary of richness to the harvest.
Greek nephros (G3510) carries the same double sense into Revelation 2:23, he which searcheth the reins and hearts.
usage: The two kidneys, and the fat that is on them (Leviticus 3:4) — the formula of the peace offering, repeated without variation.
The fat of kidneys of wheat (Deuteronomy 32:14) — the richest of the grain, described in sacrificial terms.
The fat of the kidneys of rams (Isaiah 34:6) — the language of the altar turned into the language of judgment.

etymology: Old English lifer. Webster 1828: a viscus of considerable size, which secretes the bile. In the Authorized Version the liver appears in three settings: the sacrificial law, where the caul above the liver is burned; pagan divination, where the king of Babylon reads it; and Hebrew poetry, where it stands for the seat of life and grief.
biblical_def: The liver is one of the interior parts God claims at the altar. The refrain of Leviticus takes the caul above the liver, with the kidneys (Leviticus 3:4), and at the consecration of Aaron Moses took all the fat that was upon the inwards, and the caul above the liver, and the two kidneys and burned them (Leviticus 8:16). But the liver also marks the boundary between the worship of the LORD and the arts of the nations. When Nebuchadnezzar stood at the parting of the way to choose his road, he made his arrows bright, he consulted with images, he looked in the liver (Ezekiel 21:21). That is hepatoscopy, the reading of an animal’s liver for omens, and Scripture records it as what a pagan king does when he wants to know the future without knowing God. In Hebrew poetry the liver is the deep seat of life and sorrow. Jeremiah in Lamentations says my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people (Lamentations 2:11), and Proverbs warns the young man following the strange woman that he goes on till a dart strike through his liver (Proverbs 7:23). The same organ, then: given to God at the altar, abused by the diviner, and wounded by sin.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LIVER as a viscus of considerable size, situated in the right hypochondrium, whose office is to secrete the bile. The biblical uses are sacrificial, divinatory, and poetic — the last treating the liver as the seat of life and grief.
webster_full: LIVER, n. — A viscus of considerable size and of a reddish brown color, situated in the right hypochondrium, whose office is to secrete the bile.
Anciently the liver was regarded as the seat of love and of the passions, and among the heathen its inspection was a principal branch of divination.
Webster’s second note is exactly Ezekiel 21:21. What the nations read for omens, Israel was to burn on the altar — the same organ, one people surrendering it and another interrogating it.
scriptures: Leviticus 3:4
And the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away.
Leviticus 8:16
And he took all the fat that was upon the inwards, and the caul above the liver, and the two kidneys, and their fat, and Moses burned it upon the altar.
Ezekiel 21:21
For the king of Babylon stood at the parting of the way, at the head of the two ways, to use divination: he made his arrows bright, he consulted with images, he looked in the liver.
Lamentations 2:11

Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city.
Proverbs 7:23
Till a dart strike through his liver; as a bird hasteth to the snare, and knoweth not that it is for his life.
corruption_summary: The corruption named in the text itself is divination — the attempt to read the future out of an animal’s interior rather than receive it from God’s word — and it has modern descendants wherever guidance is sought by signs, omens, and techniques instead of by Scripture and prayer.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 21:21 is a photograph of paganism at a decision point. The king has two roads and no God, so he shakes arrows, questions images, and inspects a liver. The Old Testament forbids every element of that procedure to Israel: There shall not be found among you any one that… useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch (Deuteronomy 18:10). The prohibition is not superstition about entrails; it is a claim about where knowledge of God’s purposes comes from. Israel had the word and the priest and the covenant. To read a liver was to say those were insufficient.

The descendants are not always exotic. Wherever a Christian seeks direction by opening the Bible at random, by fleeces, by numerology in dates, or by the interpretation of a leader’s dream, the structure of Ezekiel 21:21 has reappeared with better manners: a technique substituted for the word. The cure is what Deuteronomy 18 offers immediately after the prohibition — a prophet like unto Moses, which the New Testament identifies as Christ, who has spoken and whose word is written. A believer who wants to know the will of God has the Scriptures, the ordinary means of grace, and the counsel of the church; he does not need an omen, and he is forbidden one.
roots_summary: The Hebrew kabed means both liver and heavy, the organ named for its weight, and it shares its consonants with the words for glory and honour. The word for the caul is a separate term for the lobe or appendage above it.
roots_lines: Hebrew kabed (H3516) — the liver; from the root meaning to be heavy, the organ named for its weight (Leviticus 3:4; Ezekiel 21:21).
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight, honour; the same consonantal root, which is why Hebrew poetry can let the liver stand for the weighty inner self.
Hebrew yothereth (H3508) — the caul, the lobe or appendage above the liver, burned with the fat (Leviticus 8:16).
Hebrew qesem (H7081) — divination; the practice Ezekiel 21:21 records and Deuteronomy 18:10 forbids.
In Lamentations 2:11 the KJV keeps the Hebrew figure literally rather than smoothing it to heart, preserving the violence of the grief.
usage: The caul above the liver (Leviticus 3:4) — part of the fixed sacrificial formula, burned and never eaten.
He looked in the liver (Ezekiel 21:21) — divination named as the practice of a pagan king at a crossroads.
My liver is poured upon the earth (Lamentations 2:11) — the Hebrew figure for grief that reaches the deepest part of a man.

etymology: Archaic past participle of wreathe, Old English wrīthan, to twist. Webster 1828: twisted; entwined; interwoven. In the Authorized Version it belongs to the high priest’s garments — the wreathen chains of pure gold that fasten the breastplate to the ephod.
biblical_def: Wreathen work is twisted goldsmith’s work, and the KJV reserves it for one job: the chains that hold the breastplate of judgment on the high priest’s shoulders. And two chains of pure gold at the ends; of wreathen work shalt thou make them, and fasten the wreathen chains to the ouches (Exodus 28:14). The command is repeated in the making: And they made upon the breastplate chains at the ends, of wreathen work of pure gold (Exodus 39:15). The chains are not decorative. Their whole purpose is fastening: thou shalt put the two wreathen chains of gold in the two rings which are on the ends of the breastplate (Exodus 28:24), and the other ends are fixed in the ouches on the shoulderpieces (Exodus 28:25). The breastplate carried the twelve stones with the names of the tribes, and God twice says why — that Aaron bear their names upon his heart… for a memorial before the LORD continually. The wreathen chain is therefore the mechanism of intercession: twisted gold, strong because it is doubled, holding the names of the people over the heart of the man who goes in. Nothing about Israel’s standing before God hung by a single strand.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives WREATHE as to twist; to convolve; to interweave, and WREATHEN as twisted or entwined. The Exodus phrase describes gold worked as a twisted cord rather than a plain link chain.
webster_full: WREATHE, v.t. — To twist; to convolve; to wind one about another. To interweave; to entwine.
WREATHEN, pp. — Twisted; entwined; interwoven.

Applied to metal, the word describes strands worked together into a twisted cord, a form both stronger and richer than a single drawn wire — which is what pure gold bearing the weight of the breastplate would require.
scriptures: Exodus 28:14
And two chains of pure gold at the ends; of wreathen work shalt thou make them, and fasten the wreathen chains to the ouches.
Exodus 28:22
And thou shalt make upon the breastplate chains at the ends of wreathen work of pure gold.
Exodus 28:24
And thou shalt put the two wreathen chains of gold in the two rings which are on the ends of the breastplate.
Exodus 28:25
And the other two ends of the two wreathen chains thou shalt fasten in the two ouches, and put them on the shoulderpieces of the ephod before it.
Exodus 39:15
And they made upon the breastplate chains at the ends, of wreathen work of pure gold.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss here is not a false definition but a forgotten typology: the wreathen chains are the fastening of the high priest’s intercession, and the modern reader skims them as jewellery.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is archaic and uncontested. What has been lost is the reading that the Reformers and the Puritans took for granted: Exodus 28 is a portrait of Christ’s priesthood, and every fastening in it means something. The breastplate is not attached with string. It is fixed with twisted gold at four points, to rings and to ouches, so that the names of the tribes cannot slip from the priest’s heart while he is inside.

The principle to recover is the security of the intercession. Hebrews argues that our High Priest ever liveth to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25), and the Old Testament garment is the picture: the names are borne on the heart and on the shoulders, held by chains of pure gold worked double. Perseverance of the saints is not a doctrine invented at Dort; it is embroidered into the ephod. A believer who wonders whether Christ might forget him is answered by a chain.
roots_summary: The Hebrew phrase is ma'aseh 'avoth, work of cords or braided work, from a root meaning to twist or interweave; the KJV’s wreathen work renders it exactly.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'avoth (H5688) — a twisted cord, rope, or braid; in Exodus 28 the chains of the breastplate are work of cords.
Hebrew ma'aseh (H4639) — work, workmanship; the phrase names a technique, not an ornament.
Hebrew mishbetsoth (H4865) — the ouches, the settings of gold filigree into which the wreathen chains were fastened (Exodus 28:14, 25).
Hebrew choshen (H2833) — the breastplate of judgment, bearing the twelve stones with the names of the tribes.
The same root for twisting appears of thick branches and of interwoven boughs, so the image is organic before it is metallurgical.
usage: Of wreathen work shalt thou make them (Exodus 28:14) — the command; twisted gold, not plain links.
Put the two wreathen chains of gold in the two rings (Exodus 28:24) — fastening, not decoration, is the purpose.
They made upon the breastplate chains at the ends, of wreathen work of pure gold (Exodus 39:15) — the compliance recorded as carefully as the command.

etymology: English badger, a burrowing animal; Webster 1828 defines the animal. In the Authorized Version the word survives only in the fixed phrase badgers' skins, the outermost covering of the tabernacle and of its vessels in transit. The Hebrew tachash is disputed; the KJV translators chose an English animal of tough, weatherproof hide.
biblical_def: Badgers' skins are the outside of the house of God. In the list of materials for the tabernacle they come third, after gold and blue: And rams' skins dyed red, and badgers' skins, and shittim wood (Exodus 25:5). Over the fine twined linen, over the goats' hair, over the red-dyed rams' skins, God commands one more layer: a covering above of badgers' skins (Exodus 26:14). That is what Israel saw from the camp. The glory was inside; the outside was a tough, plain hide that turned the weather. When the ark and the vessels travelled, the same covering went with them: the Kohathites shall put thereon the covering of badgers' skins (Numbers 4:6), and the golden altar likewise (Numbers 4:11). The one figurative use turns it into grace: the LORD says of Jerusalem, I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers' skin (Ezekiel 16:10) — the sanctuary's own weatherproof leather made into shoes for a foundling bride. Isaiah's no form nor comeliness is the same shape of truth: the outside of what God builds is often the least impressive thing about it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BADGER as a quadruped of the genus Ursus, a burrowing animal, and notes the use of its skin for tough leather. The KJV uses the plural only of the outermost tabernacle covering, translating a Hebrew word whose animal is disputed but whose function — a durable weatherproof hide — is not.
webster_full: BADGER, n. — A quadruped of the genus Ursus, a burrowing animal of nocturnal habits; the hide is thick and tough and has been used for leather.
The Hebrew tachash has been rendered badger, seal, porpoise, dolphin, and dugong by different hands; the KJV chose an English animal known for hide durable enough to shed rain.
The exegetical point does not turn on zoology. Whatever the creature, the layer is the outermost, the toughest, and the plainest — that is what the text requires of it in every occurrence.
scriptures: Exodus 25:5
And rams' skins dyed red, and badgers' skins, and shittim wood,
Exodus 26:14
And thou shalt make a covering for the tent of rams' skins dyed red, and a covering above of badgers' skins.
Numbers 4:6
And shall put thereon the covering of badgers' skins, and shall spread over it a cloth wholly of blue, and shall put in the staves thereof.
Numbers 4:11
And upon the golden altar they shall spread a cloth of blue, and cover it with a covering of badgers' skins, and shall put to the staves thereof:
Ezekiel 16:10
I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers' skin, and I girded thee about with fine linen, and I covered thee with silk.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live danger is the opposite of redefinition: a church that reverses the tabernacle’s order, spending on the outside what God spent on the inside, and judging spiritual worth by what shows from the camp.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The scholarly argument over which animal tachash names is real but harmless; every candidate yields the same tough outer hide. The genuine problem is that the tabernacle’s order of value has been inverted in practice. God put gold and cherubim and fine twined linen where only priests would see them, and put plain leather where the whole nation would look.

The principle to recover is that God builds from the inside out. Isaiah says of the Servant that he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him (Isaiah 53:2) — badgers' skins over the glory. Paul says the same of the ministry: we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us (2 Corinthians 4:7). A congregation that measures itself by its frontage has read the tabernacle backwards. And Ezekiel 16:10 keeps the tenderness in view: the same durable hide God used to shelter His house He used to shoe a bride He had found abandoned in a field.
roots_summary: The Hebrew is tachash, an animal or hide whose identity is disputed, standing always in the phrase 'oroth techashim, skins of tachash. The related noun for skin is 'or, the same word used of the coats God made for Adam and Eve.
roots_lines: Hebrew tachash (H8476) — the animal or hide of the outermost tabernacle covering (Exodus 25:5; 26:14; Numbers 4:6); rendered badgers by the KJV.
Hebrew 'or (H5785) — skin, hide; the same noun in coats of skins for Adam and Eve (Genesis 3:21), where a covering also costs a life.
The Septuagint renders the phrase with a word for hyacinth-coloured skins, showing the animal was already uncertain before the Christian era.
The covering order runs inward to outward: fine twined linen with cherubim, goats' hair, rams' skins dyed red, badgers' skins (Exodus 26:1-14).
Ezekiel 16:10 is the only non-tabernacle occurrence, and it transfers the sanctuary material to the clothing of a rescued bride.
usage: A covering above of badgers' skins (Exodus 26:14) — the outermost of four layers; the plainest thing is what the camp sees.
The covering of badgers' skins (Numbers 4:6) — the holy things travel wrapped in the same weatherproof hide.
Shod thee with badgers' skin (Ezekiel 16:10) — sanctuary leather made into shoes for a foundling; grace in the vocabulary of the tabernacle.

etymology: From overlay, to spread or cover over. Webster 1828: covered; spread over the surface. In the Authorized Version the word is a builder’s term for plating wood with metal — almost always shittim wood with gold — and it is the standing description of the ark, the table, the altar of incense, and the walls of Solomon’s oracle.
biblical_def: To overlay is to plate a common substance with a precious one so that what is seen is gold and what bears the weight is wood. It is the dominant verb of tabernacle construction. Bezaleel made the ark and overlaid it with pure gold within and without (Exodus 37:2); the staves that carried it were shittim wood overlaid with gold (Exodus 37:4); the boards, the bars, the pillars, and the chapiters all received the same treatment (Exodus 36:34, 38). Solomon carried the practice into the temple: Solomon overlaid the house within with pure gold… and he overlaid it with gold (1 Kings 6:21). The New Testament preserves the description of the ark as overlaid round about with gold (Hebrews 9:4). Two doctrines sit in the technique. First, God is not ashamed to build with acacia — the desert wood, cheap and available, is what holds the gold. Second, the plating is within and without: the ark is gold on the face nobody sees as well as the face everyone sees. Where Scripture wants to condemn a religion of surfaces it uses the same verb of idols — a graven image the workman overlayeth with gold (Isaiah 40:19) — gilt wood, and nothing inside it at all.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives OVERLAY as to spread over; to cover the surface; also, to smother. OVERLAID is covered or spread over. The biblical use is the technical one of plating wood with metal.
webster_full: OVERLAY, v.t. — To lay over; to spread over the surface; to cover. To overwhelm; to smother.
OVERLAID, pp. — Covered; spread over; overwhelmed.
The sense in Exodus and Kings is craft, not concealment: gold beaten thin and fastened over shittim wood, so that the vessel has the strength of timber and the appearance of the glory.
scriptures: Exodus 26:32
And thou shalt hang it upon four pillars of shittim wood overlaid with gold: their hooks shall be of gold, upon the four sockets of silver.
Exodus 37:2
And he overlaid it with pure gold within and without, and made a crown of gold to it round about.
Exodus 37:4
And he made staves of shittim wood, and overlaid them with gold.
1 Kings 6:21
So Solomon overlaid the house within with pure gold: and he made a partition by the chains of gold before the oracle; and he overlaid it with gold.
Hebrews 9:4
Which had the golden censer, and the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, wherein was the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant;
corruption_summary: The verb itself is neutral; Scripture uses it both of the ark and of idols. The corruption is the gilded surface with nothing underneath — a religion, a ministry, or a life plated for the eye while the substance is untouched.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah exposes the counterfeit with the same word: The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold (Isaiah 40:19). Gilding is what idol-makers do. The difference between the ark and the idol is not the technique but the command and the contents: the ark was overlaid because God said so, and inside it were the tables of the covenant. The idol is overlaid because a man wanted it to look like a god, and inside it is wood. Our Lord makes the identical charge against the Pharisees, whited sepulchres which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones (Matthew 23:27).

The safeguard is Exodus 37:2: within and without. God required the gold on the surface nobody would ever see. That is the pattern for integrity in a minister and in a church — the same material inside the vessel as outside it. Where a ministry is built for the platform and hollow in the study, or a Christian life is plated for Sunday and bare wood on Monday, the ark has been imitated in technique and abandoned in substance. It is worth noticing what the gold is fastened to: shittim wood, common desert acacia. God is not embarrassed by ordinary material. He is offended by ordinary material pretending.
roots_summary: The Hebrew verb is tsaphah, to lay over or plate; the Greek in Hebrews 9:4 is a compound meaning covered around. Both name a craft of plating rather than an act of concealment.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsaphah (H6823) — to overlay, to plate with metal (Exodus 26:32; 37:2; 1 Kings 6:21).
Hebrew shittim (H7848) — acacia wood, the desert timber that receives the gold throughout the tabernacle.
Greek perikalupto (G4028) — to cover around; used of the ark in Hebrews 9:4, overlaid round about with gold.
The same Hebrew verb describes the gilding of idols in Isaiah 40:19, which is why the word alone settles nothing; the command does.
Exodus 37:2 specifies within and without, the phrase that rules out gilding as concealment.
usage: Overlaid it with pure gold within and without (Exodus 37:2) — the hidden face is plated as carefully as the visible one.
Pillars of shittim wood overlaid with gold (Exodus 26:32) — common desert timber under the glory, by God’s own design.
The ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold (Hebrews 9:4) — the New Testament keeps the builder’s term.

etymology: From Old French estendard, a banner, related to extendere, to spread out. Webster 1828: an ensign of war; a flag; also, a rule or measure of authority. In the Authorized Version the word is military and tribal — the four great banners under which Israel camped and marched — and once prophetic, of the standard the Spirit lifts against a flood.
biblical_def: A standard in Scripture is the banner that tells a man where he belongs. Israel in the wilderness did not camp at random: Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch (Numbers 2:2). Four standards ordered the whole camp — Judah on the east, Reuben on the south, Ephraim on the west, Dan on the north (Numbers 2:10, 18, 25) — and the same order governed the march: In the first place went the standard of the camp of the children of Judah (Numbers 10:14). Two features are doctrinal. The standards face inward: every tribe pitches by its banner, but all of them pitch about the tabernacle. Identity within the covenant people is real and ordered, and it is organized around the presence of God rather than against the other tribes. And the standard governs both rest and movement; a man knew where to sleep and when to march by the same flag. The prophetic use lifts the figure to God Himself: When the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him (Isaiah 59:19).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives STANDARD as an ensign of war; the flag of a troop or company; and, in a second sense, that which is established by authority as a rule or measure — a standard of weight, of value, of faith. Both senses are alive in English; the KJV uses the first.
webster_full: STANDARD, n. — An ensign of war; a staff with a flag or colors; the ensign of a regiment or troop.
That which is established by sovereign power as a rule or measure; as, a standard of weights and measures; a standard of value.
Hence, a test or criterion by which anything is tried — a standard of faith, a standard of morals.
The KJV’s use is uniformly the banner. But the second sense is not foreign to the theology: a people gathered under one ensign around one tabernacle is a people governed by one rule.
scriptures: Numbers 1:52
And the children of Israel shall pitch their tents, every man by his own camp, and every man by his own standard, throughout their hosts.
Numbers 2:2
Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch.
Numbers 2:10
On the south side shall be the standard of the camp of Reuben according to their armies: and the captain of the children of Reuben shall be Elizur the son of Shedeur.
Numbers 10:14
In the first place went the standard of the camp of the children of Judah according to their armies: and over his host was Nahshon the son of Amminadab.
Isaiah 59:19

So shall they fear the name of the LORD from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun. When the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him.
corruption_summary: The word is corrupted when the banner is detached from the tabernacle — when tribal identity becomes an end in itself and the camp is organized around what distinguishes the tribes rather than around the God at the centre.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 2:2 gives both halves of the order and the modern age keeps only one. Every man pitches by his own standard — identity is real, particular, and inherited, and Scripture does not dissolve it. But every standard pitches about the tabernacle of the congregation, and that is the half now routinely dropped. Where the church is arranged into caucuses whose banners face outward, and where the question “which group are you” governs more than the question “whose presence are we gathered around,” the camp of Numbers 2 has been rebuilt without its centre. Paul settles the ordering in 1 Corinthians 1:12-13: every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos… Is Christ divided?

The second corruption is the flattening of the standard into a preference. Isaiah 59:19 has the Spirit of the LORD lifting a standard against an invading flood; that is a war banner, planted where a line will be held. A church that has no standard has not become welcoming; it has become undefended. The confessions serve exactly this function — the 1689 is a banner raised so that a congregation knows what it is gathered around and where the line runs when the flood comes in.
roots_summary: Two Hebrew words lie behind the English. Degel is the tribal standard of Numbers; nes is the raised signal or pole, the word behind Isaiah’s standard and behind the name Jehovah-nissi.
roots_lines: Hebrew degel (H1714) — a banner or standard; the four tribal ensigns of the wilderness camp (Numbers 1:52; 2:2, 10; 10:14).
Hebrew 'oth (H226) — a sign or ensign; paired with degel in Numbers 2:2 as the ensign of their father's house.
Hebrew nes (H5251) — a pole, signal, or raised standard (Isaiah 59:19; Isaiah 11:10, the root lifted for an ensign of the people).
Hebrew Yahweh-nissi (Exodus 17:15) — the LORD my banner, the altar Moses built after Amalek; the same nes.
The Song of Solomon uses degel of love itself: his banner over me was love (Song of Solomon 2:4).
usage: Every man by his own standard (Numbers 1:52) — order in the camp, not uniformity; each tribe knows its place.
Far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch (Numbers 2:2) — the banners face a centre.
The Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him (Isaiah 59:19) — the war banner God plants when the enemy comes in like a flood.

etymology: From Middle English bothe, a temporary dwelling; Webster 1828: a house or shed built of boards, boughs of trees, or other slight materials, for a temporary residence. In the Authorized Version booths renders the Hebrew succoth, the leafy shelters Israel was commanded to live in for seven days every seventh month.
biblical_def: A booth is a shelter that will not last the year, and God commanded His people to live in one on purpose. Ye shall dwell in booths seven days; all that are Israelites born shall dwell in booths (Leviticus 23:42), and the reason is given in the next breath: That your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt (Leviticus 23:43). The feast is a memory exercise with a roof. A settled nation in walled cities is required, once a year, to sleep under branches, so that the children ask why and the fathers answer with the exodus. When the law was rediscovered under Ezra the people obeyed at once: And all the congregation of them that were come again out of the captivity made booths, and sat under the booths… And there was very great gladness (Nehemiah 8:17). The word first appears where Jacob made booths for his cattle and named the place Succoth (Genesis 33:17). The doctrine is pilgrimage. Israel’s permanence was never in its architecture, and the New Testament keeps the figure — the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us is literally tabernacled, and Peter on the mount wanted to build three booths and was corrected.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BOOTH as a house or shed built of boards, boughs of trees, or other slight materials, for a temporary residence. The KJV uses the plural for the shelters of the Feast of Tabernacles and for Jacob’s cattle-sheds at Succoth.
webster_full: BOOTH, n. — A house or shed built of boards, boughs of trees, or other slight materials, for a temporary residence.
Also, a stall or temporary shelter erected in a market or fair.

Webster’s definition contains the theology by accident: the material is slight and the residence is temporary. That is exactly what God required Israel to inhabit one week a year, and exactly what He was teaching them about their tenure in the land.
scriptures: Leviticus 23:42
Ye shall dwell in booths seven days; all that are Israelites born shall dwell in booths:
Leviticus 23:43
That your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
Nehemiah 8:14
And they found written in the law which the LORD had commanded by Moses, that the children of Israel should dwell in booths in the feast of the seventh month:
Nehemiah 8:17

And all the congregation of them that were come again out of the captivity made booths, and sat under the booths: for since the days of Jeshua the son of Nun unto that day had not the children of Israel done so. And there was very great gladness.
He buildeth his house as a moth, and as a booth that the keeper maketh.
corruption_summary: The booth is corrupted when the feast becomes folklore — a harvest festival with the exodus removed — and when a settled, comfortable church quietly abandons the doctrine that its people are strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the emptying of the reason. Leviticus 23:43 states the purpose without ambiguity: that the generations may know what God did in bringing Israel out of Egypt. Detach the branches from the redemption and the week becomes a seasonal celebration of the ingathering, which is how the feast has often been kept and how it is most often explained now. Scripture never lets the harvest stand alone. The joy of Nehemiah 8:17 is not agricultural satisfaction; it is a people who had just heard the law read and understood what they had been given back.

The second corruption is settled Christianity. Hebrews describes the patriarchs as those who confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth (Hebrews 11:13), dwelling in tabernacles while looking for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God. A church that has quietly concluded its situation is permanent will not preach that text with a straight face. The booth is God’s annual correction: one week under branches, in a house that could not survive a winter, so that a man knows the difference between where he lives and where he is going. Peter’s instinct on the mount — let us make three tabernacles — was to make the glory permanent too early, and the cloud interrupted him.
roots_summary: The Hebrew is sukkah, a booth or thicket-shelter, plural succoth, which is also the place name Jacob gave. The Greek New Testament word for the same shelter is skene, the word behind tabernacled in John 1:14.
roots_lines: Hebrew sukkah (H5521) — a booth, hut, or leafy shelter (Leviticus 23:42; Nehemiah 8:17; Job 27:18).
Hebrew Succoth (H5523) — the place named for the booths Jacob built for his cattle (Genesis 33:17), and Israel’s first station out of Egypt.
Hebrew chag ha-succoth — the Feast of Booths, the KJV’s Feast of Tabernacles, the seventh-month feast of Leviticus 23.
Greek skene (G4633) — a tent or booth; Peter’s three tabernacles on the mount of transfiguration (Matthew 17:4).
Greek skenoo (G4637) — to pitch a tent, to tabernacle; the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us (John 1:14).
usage: Ye shall dwell in booths seven days (Leviticus 23:42) — obedience that requires leaving the house.
That your generations may know (Leviticus 23:43) — the feast exists to provoke the child’s question and the father’s answer.
Made booths, and sat under the booths… there was very great gladness (Nehemiah 8:17) — recovered obedience produces joy, not gloom.
